doc_wheat_agronomy_01_c01.title: Wheat Sowing, Seed Rate and Agronomic Management
doc_wheat_agronomy_01_c01.license: Government Open Data / Public Agricultural Extension
doc_wheat_agronomy_01_c01.text: Optimal sowing time for irrigated timely sown wheat in the Indo-Gangetic Plains is the first fortnight of November (November 1 to November 15). For timely sown conditions, a seed rate of 100 kg per hectare is recommended. In late-sown conditions (after November 25), the seed rate should be increased to 125 kg per hectare to compensate for reduced tillering caused by shorter winter duration. Spacing between rows should be maintained at 20 to 22.5 cm with a sowing depth of 4 to 5 cm. Recommended high-yielding disease-resistant wheat varieties include HD-2967, HD-3086 (Pusa Gautami), DBW-187 (Karan Vandana), and DBW-303 (Karan Vaishnavi). Seed treatment prior to sowing with Trichoderma viride at 4 g/kg seed or Carbendazim at 2 g/kg seed is essential to prevent seed-borne and soil-borne fungal pathogens.

doc_wheat_irrigation_02_c01.title: Wheat Irrigation Scheduling and Critical Water Stages
doc_wheat_irrigation_02_c01.text: Wheat requires 4 to 6 irrigations depending on winter rainfall and soil water retention. The single most critical irrigation stage is the Crown Root Initiation (CRI) stage, which occurs 20 to 25 days after sowing (DAS). Withholding irrigation at the CRI stage can reduce final grain yield by 25 to 35 percent due to poor tillering. Subsequent critical stages in order of priority include: Tillering stage (40-45 DAS), Jointing stage (60-65 DAS), Flowering stage (80-85 DAS), Milk stage (100-105 DAS), and Dough stage (115-120 DAS). Light, frequent irrigations are preferred over heavy flooding. Avoid irrigation during high wind speeds at grain filling to prevent lodging of the standing crop.

doc_wheat_disease_rust_03_c01.title: Wheat Rust Diseases: Yellow, Brown, and Black Rust Management
doc_wheat_disease_rust_03_c01.text: Wheat yellow rust (stripe rust), caused by Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici, poses severe risks under cool (10-18 deg C) and high humidity conditions. Symptoms appear as yellow-orange uredinial pustules arranged in linear stripes along the leaf blade. Brown rust (Puccinia triticina) forms scattered round brown pustules and thrives in warmer temperatures (20-25 deg C). Upon initial rust detection, immediately spray Propiconazole 25% EC (Tilt) or Tebuconazole 25.9% EC at 1.0 ml per litre of water (500 ml dissolved in 500 litres water per hectare). A follow-up spray after 15 days is recommended if weather conditions remain overcast and humid. Avoid excessive nitrogen application as lush vegetative growth increases rust susceptibility.

doc_wheat_disease_karnal_bunt_04_c01.title: Karnal Bunt and Loose Smut of Wheat
doc_wheat_disease_karnal_bunt_04_c01.text: Karnal bunt, caused by Tilletia indica (syn. Neovossia indica), infects wheat florets during the flowering stage under cloudy, humid conditions. Infected grains show partial conversion into black powdery teliospore masses emitting a distinct rotten fish odor due to trimethylamine. Management requires avoiding susceptible varieties, practicing crop rotation with non-host crops like mustard or chickpea, and applying a single foliar spray of Propiconazole 25% EC at 0.1% at the boot leaf to early earhead emergence stage. Loose smut, caused by Ustilago tritici, turns entire ears into black powdery masses; it is controlled by seed treatment with Carboxin 37.5% + Thiram 37.5% (Vitavax Power) at 2.5 g/kg seed.

doc_wheat_fertilizer_05_c01.title: Nutrient Management and Fertilizer Regimes for High-Yield Wheat
doc_wheat_fertilizer_05_c01.text: General recommended fertilizer dose for irrigated high-yielding wheat varieties is 120-150 kg Nitrogen, 60 kg Phosphorus (P2O5), and 40 kg Potassium (K2O) per hectare. Apply full dose of phosphorus, potassium, and one-third of nitrogen as basal dressing at the time of sowing. The remaining two-thirds of nitrogen must be split into two equal top dressings: first at the first irrigation (CRI stage, 21-25 DAS) and second at the first node/jointing stage (45-50 DAS). In soils deficient in zinc, apply 25 kg Zinc Sulfate (ZnSO4 21%) per hectare as basal application once every two years. Do not mix zinc sulfate directly with phosphatic fertilizers such as DAP to avoid precipitation of insoluble zinc phosphate.

doc_rice_agronomy_06_c01.title: Rice Transplanting, Direct Seeding, and Water Regimes
doc_rice_agronomy_06_c01.text: Rice nursery should be sown in May-June for Kharif season. Seedlings are ready for transplanting at 20 to 25 days of age when they attain 4 to 5 leaves. Transplant 2 to 3 seedlings per hill at a spacing of 20 x 15 cm or 20 x 10 cm, maintaining a shallow transplanting depth of 2 to 3 cm. For Direct Seeded Rice (DSR), use 20 to 25 kg certified seed per hectare sown with a seed-cum-fertilizer drill at 2 to 3 cm depth. In transplanted rice, maintain 2 to 5 cm shallow water ponding for the first 15 days to suppress weeds, followed by Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) water management. AWD saves up to 30 percent irrigation water without penalizing yield. Drain water 10 to 15 days before harvest.

doc_rice_disease_blast_07_c01.title: Rice Blast and Bacterial Leaf Blight Management
doc_rice_disease_blast_07_c01.text: Rice blast, caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (Pyricularia oryzae), causes spindle-shaped lesions with brown borders and grayish-white centers on leaves (leaf blast) and rotting of the panicle base (neck blast). For blast management, spray Tricyclazole 75% WP at 0.6 g/L or Isoprothiolane 40% EC at 1.5 ml/L at disease onset. Bacterial Leaf Blight (BLB), caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae, exhibits wavy straw-colored margins starting from leaf tips downwards. For BLB, spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP at 2.5 g/L mixed with Streptocycline or Plantomycin at 0.1 g/L. Avoid high nitrogen top-dressing during active blast or BLB outbreaks as free nitrogen aggravates tissue susceptibility.

doc_rice_disease_sheath_blight_08_c01.title: Rice Sheath Blight and False Smut Management
doc_rice_disease_sheath_blight_08_c01.text: Rice Sheath Blight, caused by Rhizoctonia solani, causes oval, greenish-grey lesions on leaf sheaths near the water level, which coalesce into serpentine patches. Manage by avoiding excess plant density and spraying Hexaconazole 5% SC at 2 ml/L or Validamycin 3% L at 2.5 ml/L or Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC at 1 ml/L. False Smut, caused by Ustilaginoidea virens, transforms individual grains into enlarged velvety yellow-orange or greenish-black smut balls. Apply prophylactic spray of Copper Hydroxide 77% WP at 2 g/L or Trifloxystrobin 25% + Tebuconazole 50% WG at 0.4 g/L at the boot leaf stage prior to panicle emergence.

doc_rice_fertilizer_09_c01.title: Fertilizer Regimes and Zinc Management for Paddy
doc_rice_fertilizer_09_c01.text: Recommended fertilizer dose for high-yielding dwarf rice varieties is 120-150 kg N, 50-60 kg P2O5, and 40-50 kg K2O per hectare. Apply one-third nitrogen and entire phosphorus and potassium before the final puddling as basal application. Top-dress one-third nitrogen at active tillering (21-25 days after transplanting) and the remaining one-third nitrogen at panicle initiation (40-45 DAT). In zinc-deficient soils, Khaira disease manifests as rusty bronze discoloration on young leaves. Apply 25 kg Zinc Sulfate heptahydrate (21% Zn) per hectare at puddling, or spray 0.5% Zinc Sulfate + 0.25% lime solution twice at 10-day intervals upon symptom appearance.

doc_soybean_agronomy_10_c01.title: Soybean Cultivation, Inoculation, and Sowing Standards
doc_soybean_agronomy_10_c01.text: Soybean (Glycine max) is primarily cultivated in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan. Optimum sowing window is the onset of monsoon between June 15 and July 5. Sowing should be executed when at least 100 mm of cumulative rainfall is received and soil moisture reaches 10-15 cm depth. Recommended seed rate is 70 to 75 kg per hectare for bold-seeded varieties and 60 to 65 kg/ha for medium-seeded cultivars (e.g., JS 335, JS 95-60, JS 20-34, NRC 127). Row-to-row spacing should be maintained at 45 cm and plant-to-plant spacing at 5 to 7 cm. Sowing depth must not exceed 3 to 4 cm to prevent seed rotting. Seed inoculation with Bradyrhizobium japonicum and Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB) at 5 g/kg seed enhances biological nitrogen fixation.

doc_soybean_disease_11_c01.title: Soybean Rust, Yellow Mosaic Virus, and Charcoal Rot
doc_soybean_disease_11_c01.text: Soybean Asian Rust, caused by Phakopsora pachyrhizi, produces minute brown or reddish-brown polygonal lesions on lower leaves, rapidly leading to defoliation under high humidity. Spray Hexaconazole 5% EC at 1 ml/L or Propiconazole 25% EC at 1 ml/L upon early disease symptoms. Yellow Mosaic Virus (YMV), transmitted by whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), causes bright yellow patches and mosaic mottling on foliage. Whitefly vector control requires seed treatment with Thiamethoxam 30% FS at 10 ml/kg seed, followed by foliar application of Acetamiprid 20% SP at 0.3 g/L or Thiamethoxam 25% WG at 0.3 g/L. Charcoal rot (Macrophomina phaseolina) causes premature plant wilting and black microsclerotia inside split stems under hot, drought-stressed conditions.

doc_soybean_fertilizer_12_c01.title: Nutrient and Sulfur Management in Soybean
doc_soybean_fertilizer_12_c01.text: As a leguminous oilseed crop, soybean requires a starter fertilizer dose of 20-30 kg Nitrogen, 60-80 kg P2O5, and 40 kg K2O per hectare applied basal at sowing. Soybean exhibits high sulfur demand for oil and methionine synthesis; apply 20 to 30 kg elemental sulfur or 200 kg gypsum per hectare. Excess inorganic nitrogen suppresses nodulation and biological nitrogen fixation. Deep placement of phosphatic fertilizers (5 cm to the side and 5 cm below the seed line) promotes root development. Foliar spraying of 2% Urea or 1% 19:19:19 soluble fertilizer at pod initiation stage boosts seed filling and final test weight.

doc_cotton_agronomy_13_c01.title: Bt Cotton Sowing, Spacing, and Canopy Management
doc_cotton_agronomy_13_c01.text: Cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) thrives in deep black soils (vertisols) with good internal drainage. Sowing time ranges from late April to May under irrigated conditions in North India, and June-July with monsoon onset in Central and South India. Seed rate for Bt cotton hybrid is 2.0 to 2.5 kg per hectare. Recommended spacing is 90 x 45 cm or 90 x 60 cm for medium soils, and 120 x 60 cm for fertile irrigated soils. Under high-density planting system (HDPS), spacing is reduced to 60 x 10 cm or 75 x 10 cm using compact non-hybrid genotypes. Seed treatment with Imidacloprid 70% WS at 5 g/kg seed protects seedlings from sucking pests for 30-40 days after germination.

doc_cotton_disease_pests_14_c01.title: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus, Bollworms, and Pink Bollworm Management
doc_cotton_disease_pests_14_c01.text: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus (CLCuV), transmitted by whitefly, causes upward leaf curling, thickening of veins, and leaf-like enations on lower leaf surfaces. Cultivate resistant hybrids and control whitefly with Spiromesifen 22.9% SC at 1 ml/L or Pyriproxyfen 10% EC at 2 ml/L. Pink Bollworm (Pectinophora gossypiella) damages bolls by entering developing seeds, causing 'rosetted flowers' and stained lint. Management: install pheromone traps at 5 traps/ha for monitoring and 20 traps/ha for mass trapping; release Trichogramma egg parasitoids; spray Emamectin Benzoate 5% SG at 0.5 g/L or Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC at 0.3 ml/L when rosette flower infestation crosses 5 percent.

doc_cotton_fertilizer_15_c01.title: Fertilizer Schedule and Micronutrient Correction in Cotton
doc_cotton_fertilizer_15_c01.text: Fertilizer recommendation for hybrid cotton is 120-150 kg N, 60 kg P2O5, and 60 kg K2O per hectare. Nitrogen should be applied in three splits: 20% basal, 40% at squaring stage (40-45 DAS), and 40% at peak flowering/boll formation stage (70-75 DAS). Phosphorus is applied full basal, while potassium is split equally between basal and peak flowering. In black soils, magnesium and boron deficiencies cause reddening of leaves (leaf reddening syndrome). To rectify leaf reddening, spray 1% Magnesium Sulfate (MgSO4) combined with 1% Urea at 60 and 80 DAS. Foliar spray of Planofix (NAA 4.5% SL) at 4 ml in 15 L water reduces square and boll shedding.

doc_maize_agronomy_16_c01.title: Maize Cultivation, Planting Geometry, and Irrigation
doc_maize_agronomy_16_c01.text: Maize (Zea mays) is grown across Kharif, Rabi, and Spring seasons. Kharif sowing takes place in June-July, and Rabi sowing in October-November. Seed rate for hybrid maize is 20 kg per hectare, and 25 kg/ha for composites. Recommended spacing is 60 cm between rows and 20 cm between plants, maintaining a plant population of 66,000 to 83,000 plants per hectare. Sowing depth is 4 to 5 cm. Maize is highly sensitive to both waterlogging and moisture deficit. Avoid standing water around the collar region; maintain raised bed or ridge-and-furrow planting. The two critical stages for irrigation are tasseling (emergence of male inflorescence) and silking (emergence of female stigma). Moisture stress at tasseling/silking causes barren cobs.

doc_maize_disease_pest_17_c01.title: Fall Armyworm and Turcicum Leaf Blight Management in Maize
doc_maize_disease_pest_17_c01.text: Fall Armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) is an invasive voracious pest of maize. Larvae feed deep inside the leaf whorls, creating ragged shot-hole feeding marks and coarse sawdust-like frass. For early instar larvae (whorl stage), apply neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) or spray Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC at 0.4 ml/L or Emamectin Benzoate 5% SG at 0.4 g/L directed into the whorls. Turcicum Leaf Blight (Exserohilum turcicum) causes large elongated spindle-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions on foliage. Apply Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L or Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC at 1 ml/L at first disease detection.

doc_maize_fertilizer_18_c01.title: Maize Nutrition and Zinc Application Guidelines
doc_maize_fertilizer_18_c01.text: Maize is an exhaustive feeder requiring 120-150 kg N, 60-70 kg P2O5, and 40-50 kg K2O per hectare. Nitrogen must be split into three applications: 20% basal at sowing, 50% at knee-high stage (30-35 DAS), and 30% at tasseling stage (55-60 DAS). All phosphorus and potassium should be applied basal. Maize is acutely sensitive to zinc deficiency, which causes 'white bud' of maize (broad bands of bleached tissue on either side of the midrib on young leaves). Apply 25 kg/ha Zinc Sulfate (ZnSO4 21%) as basal dressing. If deficiency appears on standing crop, spray 0.5% ZnSO4 neutralized with 0.25% slaked lime.

doc_tomato_agronomy_19_c01.title: Tomato Nursery Raising, Staking, and Transplanting
doc_tomato_agronomy_19_c01.text: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is cultivated in autumn-winter and spring-summer seasons. Seed rate for determinate varieties is 400-500 g/ha, and for indeterminate F1 hybrids is 125-150 g/ha. Raise seedlings on raised nursery beds treated with Trichoderma harzianum at 10 g/m2. Transplant 25 to 30 day old seedlings at a spacing of 60 x 45 cm for determinate varieties and 90 x 45 cm for indeterminate hybrids. Indeterminate hybrids must be staked with bamboo poles and trellis wires to prevent fruit rotting from soil contact, improve pesticide coverage, and maximize marketable yield. Pruning lateral suckers improves fruit size.

doc_tomato_disease_20_c01.title: Tomato Early Blight, Late Blight, and Leaf Curl Virus
doc_tomato_disease_20_c01.text: Early Blight, caused by Alternaria solani, forms dark brown concentric rings ('target board' appearance) surrounded by chlorotic halos on older leaves. Late Blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, produces rapidly enlarging water-soaked blackish-brown lesions under cool (12-18 deg C) wet weather with white cottony mildew on the underside of leaves. For Early Blight, spray Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP at 2 g/L. For Late Blight, spray Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP (Ridomil MZ) at 2.5 g/L or Dimethomorph 50% WP at 1.5 g/L. Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (ToLCV) causes upward cupping, severe leaf stunting, and puckering; control whitefly vector using sticky yellow traps and spray Dinotefuran 20% SG at 0.3 g/L.

doc_tomato_fertilizer_21_c01.title: Tomato Fertigation and Blossom End Rot Prevention
doc_tomato_fertilizer_21_c01.text: Recommended fertilizer dose for hybrid tomato is 180-250 kg N, 100-150 kg P2O5, and 150-200 kg K2O per hectare. Under drip irrigation, apply water-soluble fertilizers in weekly splits from vegetative to fruiting stages. Blossom End Rot (BER) is a physiological disorder characterized by dark sunken leathery lesions at the blossom end of the fruit, caused by calcium deficiency in expanding fruit tissues often induced by irregular moisture supply. Prevent BER by maintaining uniform soil moisture and foliar spraying Calcium Nitrate at 0.5% (5 g/L) during active fruit set and enlargement.

doc_potato_agronomy_22_c01.title: Potato Seed Tuber Selection, Spacing, and Earthing Up
doc_potato_agronomy_22_c01.text: Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is a cool-season tuber crop. Planting time in North Indian plains is mid-October to early November. Use disease-free certified whole seed tubers weighing 40 to 50 g (30-40 mm diameter). Seed rate is 2.5 to 3.0 tonnes per hectare. Before planting, treat tubers with 3% Boric acid solution for 30 minutes to manage black scurf. Plant tubers on ridges at 60 cm row-to-row spacing and 20 cm plant-to-plant spacing at 5-7 cm depth. Earthing up should be conducted 30 to 35 days after planting when plants reach 15-20 cm height to prevent greening of developing tubers caused by solar exposure (solanine toxicity) and to facilitate optimal tuber bulking.

doc_potato_disease_23_c01.title: Potato Late Blight and Black Scurf Management
doc_potato_disease_23_c01.text: Potato Late Blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is the most destructive potato disease worldwide. Under favorable weather (temperatures 10-20 deg C and relative humidity >90%), entire fields can be decimated within days. Prophylactic application of Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/L or Propineb 70% WP at 2.5 g/L should be completed before cloud cover and rain. If infection has commenced, spray Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP at 2.5 g/L or Fenamidone 10% + Mancozeb 50% WG at 2.5 g/L. Practice dehaulming (cutting potato foliage at the base) 10-12 days before tuber harvesting to prevent spore wash onto tubers during digging.

doc_potato_fertilizer_24_c01.title: Potato Nutrient Management and Potassium Requirements
doc_potato_fertilizer_24_c01.text: Potato produces heavy biomass in short duration (90-110 days) and requires 150-180 kg N, 80-100 kg P2O5, and 120-150 kg K2O per hectare. Potassium is critical for carbohydrate translocation from foliage into tubers. Potassium sulfate (SOP) is preferred over potassium chloride (MOP) for processing potato varieties because chloride ions reduce tuber dry matter and starch content. Apply full P, full K, and half N as basal dressing in furrows below tuber level. Top-dress the remaining half N at the time of earthing up (30-35 DAP). Avoid late nitrogen application as it delays tuber maturation and prolongs skin setting.

doc_sugarcane_agronomy_25_c01.title: Sugarcane Planting Methods, Sett Treatment, and Trash Mulching
doc_sugarcane_agronomy_25_c01.text: Sugarcane (Saccharum officinarum) planting seasons are Autumn (October), Spring (February-March), and Adsali (July-August in tropical zones). Use disease-free three-budded setts from 8 to 10 month old seed nursery crops. Sett rate is 35,000 to 40,000 three-budded setts per hectare. Treat setts with Carbendazim 50% WP at 1 g/L or hot water treatment at 52 deg C for 30 minutes to eradicate systemic pathogens. Recommended furrow spacing is 90 cm to 120 cm. Trench planting and wide-row planting (120-150 cm) allow mechanization and intercropping. Trash mulching (spreading dried sugarcane leaves at 3-5 tonnes/ha in inter-row spaces) conserves soil moisture, regulates soil temperature, and suppresses troublesome weeds.

doc_sugarcane_disease_26_c01.title: Sugarcane Red Rot and Smut Management Strategies
doc_sugarcane_disease_26_c01.text: Red Rot, caused by Colletotrichum falcatum, is the 'cancer of sugarcane'. Symptoms include yellowing and drooping of crown leaves followed by complete drying of the spindle. Longitudinal splitting of infected canes reveals red discoloration with crosswise white patches and an alcoholic odor. Management: strictly avoid planting setts from infected fields; cultivate red-rot resistant varieties such as Co-0238 (monitor for strain breakdown), Co-98014, and Co-0118; practice crop rotation with paddy or green manure crops; eradicate diseased clumps promptly. Sugarcane Smut (Sporisorium scitamineum) produces a long whip-like black dusty structure from the terminal shoot; rogue out smutted whips in polythene bags and burn them.

doc_sugarcane_fertilizer_27_c01.title: Sugarcane Nutrition, Ratoon Management, and Iron Chlorosis
doc_sugarcane_fertilizer_27_c01.text: Sugarcane requires 250-300 kg N, 80-100 kg P2O5, and 120-150 kg K2O per hectare in tropical regions (150-200 kg N in sub-tropics). Entire P and K are applied basal. Nitrogen is applied in splits: 25% at planting, 50% during tillering (60-90 days), and 25% at final earthing up (120-150 days). For ratoon sugarcane, increase nitrogen dose by 20-25 percent and apply immediately after stubble shaving. Iron chlorosis is widespread in calcareous soils, causing interveinal yellowing of young leaves. Correct iron deficiency by foliar spraying 1% Ferrous Sulfate (FeSO4) mixed with 0.1% citric acid twice at 10-day intervals.

doc_weather_irrigation_climate_28_c01.title: Agrometeorological Practices: Frost, Heat Waves, and Spraying Windows
doc_weather_irrigation_climate_28_c01.text: Agrometeorological management mitigates severe weather hazards on field crops. To mitigate winter radiation frost (when temperatures approach 0 to 4 deg C), apply light evening irrigation to elevate soil thermal capacity and release latent heat; maintain smoke/smudge fires on upwind boundaries of orchards and potato fields. In case of forecast high temperatures/heatwaves during wheat flowering or grain filling (terminal heat stress), apply light micro-sprinkler irrigation or spray Potassium Nitrate (13:0:45) at 1% or Salicylic Acid at 100 ppm to boost osmotic tolerance. Pesticide and foliar fertilizer sprays require a rain-free window of at least 24 hours and wind speeds below 10 km/h to prevent spray drift and chemical wash-off.

doc_weather_monsoon_drainage_29_c01.title: Monsoon Inundation, Soil Aeration, and Post-Flood Recovery
doc_weather_monsoon_drainage_29_c01.text: Excessive monsoon precipitation and waterlogging impair root respiration and induce soil denitrification. Except for paddy, field crops like maize, cotton, and soybean cannot tolerate prolonged root submergence beyond 24 to 48 hours. Construct broad bed furrows (BBF) or ridge-furrow land configurations to facilitate rapid surface drainage. Following flood recession, aerate soil by shallow hoeing once the soil attains workable moisture; apply a foliar booster spray of 1 to 2% Urea or 19:19:19 to rapidly restore chlorophyll synthesis and compensate for root nutrient uptake paralysis.

doc_soil_organic_carbon_salinity_30_c01.title: Soil Health Management, Salinity Reclamation, and Organic Amendments
doc_soil_organic_carbon_salinity_30_c01.text: Sustained soil health requires maintaining soil organic carbon (SOC) levels above 0.75%. In tropical soils where SOC has depleted below 0.4%, incorporate 8 to 10 tonnes Farm Yard Manure (FYM) or 5 tonnes vermicompost per hectare annually, or grow Dhaincha (Sesbania aculeata) / Sunnhemp as green manure and incorporate at 45-50 days. In sodic/alkaline soils (pH > 8.5, ESP > 15%), apply gypsum based on gypsum requirement (GR) followed by leaching with good quality water. In saline soils (EC > 4 dS/m), provide subsurface drainage and leach soluble salts with excess irrigation water. Always test soil every 2 to 3 years to balance NPK ratios according to 4R nutrient stewardship (Right source, Right rate, Right time, Right place).

doc_wheat_crop_advice_031_c01.title: Wheat - Nursery Management and Seedbed Preparation
doc_wheat_crop_advice_031_c01.text: Wheat - Nursery Management and Seedbed Preparation: In commercial production of wheat, Prepare raised nursery beds of 1 meter width and 15 cm elevation with well-rotted FYM. Solarize nursery soil or treat with Trichoderma harzianum at 10 g/m2 to prevent pre- and post-emergence damping-off caused by Pythium and Rhizoctonia spp. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_crop_advice_032_c01.title: Wheat - Sowing Depth, Spacing and Plant Geometry
doc_wheat_crop_advice_032_c01.text: Wheat - Sowing Depth, Spacing and Plant Geometry: In commercial production of wheat, Maintain optimal planting depth and geometry recommended for the agro-climatic zone. Shallow planting promotes rapid seedling emergence, while uniform row-to-row spacing minimizes inter-plant competition for solar radiation and soil moisture. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_crop_advice_033_c01.title: Wheat - Irrigation Scheduling and Critical Moisture Stages
doc_wheat_crop_advice_033_c01.text: Wheat - Irrigation Scheduling and Critical Moisture Stages: In commercial production of wheat, Schedule irrigations at critical moisture-sensitive growth stages to avoid drought-induced yield penalties. Utilize moisture sensors or tensiometers to schedule irrigations at 50% available soil moisture depletion. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_soil_fertilizer_034_c01.title: Wheat - Nitrogen Management and Split Application
doc_wheat_soil_fertilizer_034_c01.text: Wheat - Nitrogen Management and Split Application: In commercial production of wheat, Split inorganic nitrogen into basal and top-dressing applications coinciding with active vegetative and reproductive initiation. Avoid excessive single-dose nitrogen applications to prevent leaching losses, volatilization, and succulent foliage susceptible to pests. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_soil_fertilizer_035_c01.title: Wheat - Phosphorus and Potassium Basal Nutrition
doc_wheat_soil_fertilizer_035_c01.text: Wheat - Phosphorus and Potassium Basal Nutrition: In commercial production of wheat, Apply full doses of phosphatic and potassic fertilizers as basal placement in furrows 5 cm below the seed. Deep placement encourages root proliferation and facilitates early establishment of a robust root system. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_soil_fertilizer_036_c01.title: Wheat - Micronutrient Management and Foliar Feeding
doc_wheat_soil_fertilizer_036_c01.text: Wheat - Micronutrient Management and Foliar Feeding: In commercial production of wheat, Address micronutrient deficiencies (zinc, boron, iron, sulfur) through soil testing. Foliar sprays of chelated micronutrients at early growth or pre-flowering stages rapidly rectify tissue chlorosis and promote pollen viability. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_crop_advice_037_c01.title: Wheat - Integrated Weed Management and Herbicides
doc_wheat_crop_advice_037_c01.text: Wheat - Integrated Weed Management and Herbicides: In commercial production of wheat, Critical weed competition period occurs between 15 and 45 days after sowing. Combine pre-emergence herbicides like Pendimethalin 30% EC with mechanical hoeing and mulching to suppress monocot and dicot weeds while preventing herbicide resistance. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_disease_038_c01.title: Wheat - Major Fungal Diseases and Chemical Control
doc_wheat_disease_038_c01.text: Wheat - Major Fungal Diseases and Chemical Control: In commercial production of wheat, Scout weekly for fungal foliar blights, rusts, and leaf spots. Apply registered systemic fungicides (e.g., Triazoles, Strobilurins) at recommended dilutions upon crossing economic threshold levels. Rotate chemical classes to prevent fungal resistance. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_disease_039_c01.title: Wheat - Bacterial and Viral Pathogen Management
doc_wheat_disease_039_c01.text: Wheat - Bacterial and Viral Pathogen Management: In commercial production of wheat, Bacterial and viral infections require preventive sanitation, vector control, and clean certified planting material. For bacterial diseases, apply copper bactericides combined with antibiotic formulations; for viral diseases, eliminate insect vectors using sticky traps and selective insecticides. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_disease_040_c01.text: Wheat - Insect Pests, Borers and Vector Suppression: In commercial production of wheat, Monitor pest incidence using species-specific pheromone traps and light traps. Target early instar larvae with biorational insecticides like Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or insect growth regulators before larvae bore into stem or fruit tissues. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_disease_041_c01.title: Wheat - Biological Control and Microbial Bioagents
doc_wheat_disease_041_c01.text: Wheat - Biological Control and Microbial Bioagents: In commercial production of wheat, Conserve natural enemies including parasitoid wasps, ladybird beetles, and hoverfly larvae. Inoculate root zones or foliage with entomopathogenic fungi (Beauveria bassiana, Metarhizium anisopliae) at 5 g/L to suppress subterranean and foliar insect pests naturally. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_weather_context_042_c01.text: Wheat - Agrometeorology and Weather Spray Windows: In commercial production of wheat, Ensure chemical sprays are applied during calm morning hours with wind speeds under 10 km/h and a confirmed rain-free window of 24 hours. High ambient humidity combined with warm temperatures accelerates foliar pathogen sporulation. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_wheat_weather_context_043_c01.title: Wheat - Drought and Heat Stress Mitigation
doc_wheat_weather_context_043_c01.text: Wheat - Drought and Heat Stress Mitigation: In commercial production of wheat, Alleviate abiotic stress by foliar spraying anti-transpirants or 1% Potassium Nitrate (13:0:45) and Salicylic Acid (100 ppm). doc_wheat_weather_context_044_c01.title: Wheat - Waterlogging, Drainage and Post-Flood Care
doc_wheat_weather_context_044_c01.text: Wheat - Waterlogging, Drainage and Post-Flood Care: In commercial production of wheat, Field crops require prompt surface drainage through field ditches within 24 hours of inundation to prevent root asphyxiation. doc_rice_crop_advice_047_c01.text: Rice - Sowing Depth, Spacing and Plant Geometry: In commercial production of rice, Maintain optimal planting depth and geometry recommended for the agro-climatic zone. doc_rice_crop_advice_048_c01.text: Rice - Irrigation Scheduling and Critical Moisture Stages: In commercial production of rice, Schedule irrigations at critical moisture-sensitive growth stages to avoid drought-induced yield penalties. doc_rice_soil_fertilizer_049_c01.title: Rice - Nitrogen Management and Split Application
doc_rice_soil_fertilizer_049_c01.text: Rice - Nitrogen Management and Split Application: In commercial production of rice, Split inorganic nitrogen into basal and top-dressing applications coinciding with active vegetative and reproductive initiation. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_rice_soil_fertilizer_050_c01.text: Rice - Phosphorus and Potassium Basal Nutrition: In commercial production of rice, Apply full doses of phosphatic and potassic fertilizers as basal placement in furrows 5 cm below the seed. doc_rice_soil_fertilizer_051_c01.text: Rice - Micronutrient Management and Foliar Feeding: In commercial production of rice, Address micronutrient deficiencies (zinc, boron, iron, sulfur) through soil testing. Foliar sprays of chelated micronutrients at early growth or pre-flowering stages rapidly rectify tissue chlorosis and promote pollen viability. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_maize_disease_100_c01.title: Maize - Insect Pests, Borers and Vector Suppression
doc_maize_disease_100_c01.text: Maize - Insect Pests, Borers and Vector Suppression: In commercial production of maize, Monitor pest incidence using species-specific pheromone traps and light traps. Target early instar larvae with biorational insecticides like Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or insect growth regulators before larvae bore into stem or fruit tissues. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_maize_disease_101_c01.title: Maize - Biological Control and Microbial Bioagents
doc_maize_disease_101_c01.text: Maize - Biological Control and Microbial Bioagents: In commercial production of maize, Conserve natural enemies including parasitoid wasps, ladybird beetles, and hoverfly larvae. Inoculate root zones or foliage with entomopathogenic fungi (Beauveria bassiana, Metarhizium anisopliae) at 5 g/L to suppress subterranean and foliar insect pests naturally. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_maize_weather_context_102_c01.title: Maize - Agrometeorology and Weather Spray Windows
doc_maize_weather_context_102_c01.text: Maize - Agrometeorology and Weather Spray Windows: In commercial production of maize, Ensure chemical sprays are applied during calm morning hours with wind speeds under 10 km/h and a confirmed rain-free window of 24 hours. High ambient humidity combined with warm temperatures accelerates foliar pathogen sporulation. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_maize_weather_context_103_c01.title: Maize - Drought and Heat Stress Mitigation
doc_maize_weather_context_103_c01.text: Maize - Drought and Heat Stress Mitigation: In commercial production of maize, Alleviate abiotic stress by foliar spraying anti-transpirants or 1% Potassium Nitrate (13:0:45) and Salicylic Acid (100 ppm). Maintain protective straw mulching to reduce soil evaporative losses and regulate root zone temperature. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_maize_weather_context_104_c01.title: Maize - Waterlogging, Drainage and Post-Flood Care
doc_maize_weather_context_104_c01.text: Maize - Waterlogging, Drainage and Post-Flood Care: In commercial production of maize, Field crops require prompt surface drainage through field ditches within 24 hours of inundation to prevent root asphyxiation. Following drainage, apply light inter-cultivation to aerate the soil and spray 1-2% Urea to stimulate recovery. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_maize_crop_advice_105_c01.title: Maize - Harvesting Maturity and Post-Harvest Sanitation
doc_maize_crop_advice_105_c01.text: Maize - Harvesting Maturity and Post-Harvest Sanitation: In commercial production of maize, Harvest crop at physiological maturity when grain moisture reaches safe thresholds (14-16% for cereals). Dry produce to 10-12% moisture before storage in hermetic bags or fumigated bins to prevent Aspergillus flavus and storage insect infestation. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_tomato_crop_advice_106_c01.text: Tomato - Nursery Management and Seedbed Preparation: In commercial production of tomato, Prepare raised nursery beds of 1 meter width and 15 cm elevation with well-rotted FYM. doc_tomato_crop_advice_107_c01.text: Tomato - Sowing Depth, Spacing and Plant Geometry: In commercial production of tomato, Maintain optimal planting depth and geometry recommended for the agro-climatic zone. Shallow planting promotes rapid seedling emergence, while uniform row-to-row spacing minimizes inter-plant competition for solar radiation and soil moisture. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_tomato_crop_advice_108_c01.title: Tomato - Irrigation Scheduling and Critical Moisture Stages
doc_tomato_crop_advice_108_c01.text: Tomato - Irrigation Scheduling and Critical Moisture Stages: In commercial production of tomato, Schedule irrigations at critical moisture-sensitive growth stages to avoid drought-induced yield penalties. Utilize moisture sensors or tensiometers to schedule irrigations at 50% available soil moisture depletion. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_tomato_soil_fertilizer_109_c01.title: Tomato - Nitrogen Management and Split Application
doc_tomato_soil_fertilizer_109_c01.text: Tomato - Nitrogen Management and Split Application: In commercial production of tomato, Split inorganic nitrogen into basal and top-dressing applications coinciding with active vegetative and reproductive initiation. Avoid excessive single-dose nitrogen applications to prevent leaching losses, volatilization, and succulent foliage susceptible to pests. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_tomato_soil_fertilizer_110_c01.title: Tomato - Phosphorus and Potassium Basal Nutrition
doc_tomato_soil_fertilizer_110_c01.text: Tomato - Phosphorus and Potassium Basal Nutrition: In commercial production of tomato, Apply full doses of phosphatic and potassic fertilizers as basal placement in furrows 5 cm below the seed. Deep placement encourages root proliferation and facilitates early establishment of a robust root system. Adhere strictly to recommended safety withdrawal intervals before harvest.

doc_tomato_soil_fertilizer_111_c01.text: Tomato - Micronutrient Management and Foliar Feeding: In commercial production of tomato, Address micronutrient deficiencies (zinc, boron, iron, sulfur) through soil testing. Foliar sprays of chelated micronutrients at early growth or pre-flowering stages rapidly rectify tissue chlorosis and promote pollen viability.
